topic: A Phone Screen Feels Your Finger Without Pressure

The opening frame shows the object already moving. Start the mechanism about 5 seconds in, at the clue scene. YouTube title seed: How Does Your Phone Screen Know It's Your Finger?
YouTube description seed: Ever tried texting with gloves on? Guess what else can tap your screen. #TellMeWhyyyyyy #Shorts
The central fact: The screen notices when a finger changes the charge on its tiny grid, not how hard you press.
The later surprise: That's why a spoon or a hot dog can tap it, but wool gloves can't.
The very first frame shows a phone lying flat on a wooden table while a gloved fingertip taps the screen again and again, and nothing happens. It is already moving in the first frame, and nothing in the first second gives the answer away.
What changes inside each 6s clip:
Scene 1 (contradiction, 0-6s): Opening: the gloved tap does nothing. About 2s in, a harder press, still nothing; about 4s in, the glove comes off.
Scene 2 (clue, 6-12s): Mechanism starts about 5s in. A bare fingertip barely brushes the glass and an app opens; about 2-3s later, a feather-light swipe scrolls a page; then the finger hovers just above the glass.
Scene 3 (mechanism, 12-18s): Macro of the screen glass at an angle so the faint grid of the touch layer catches the light (real parts or physical props only, no animation or cutaway graphics); about 2s in, a fingertip lands on one spot; about 4s in, the touch point appears under it.
Scene 4 (second_reveal, 18-24s): A metal spoon tip taps and opens an app; about 2s in, a hot dog swipes the screen and it scrolls; about 4s in, a wool-gloved finger tries again and fails.
Scene 5 (payoff, 24-30s): A person laughs and puts the hot dog down; about 3s in, return to the exact opening: the same phone on the same wooden table with the gloved fingertip tapping and nothing happening, same framing as scene 1's first frame, so it loops.
Fact boundaries: Applies to capacitive screens such as most smartphones; older pressure-based resistive screens work differently. Do not say electricity flows out of your body or that the screen shocks you. Touch-friendly gloves exist; do not say all gloves fail.

facts.statement: A phone's capacitive screen is covered in a grid of tiny electrodes holding a steady charge; a fingertip near the glass changes the capacitance at that spot, and the phone reads that change as a touch.
It is not measuring how hard you press; a light touch from something conductive enough works.
Wool gloves fail because they don't conduct well and keep the finger too far from the glass, while a metal spoon or even a hot dog can work because it disturbs the charge like a finger does.
